fetched_contents.text: Infant jaundice - Diagnosis & treatment Diagnosis A healthcare professional will likely diagnose infant jaundice by checking a baby's appearance. However, it's still necessary to measure the level of bilirubin in a baby's blood. The level of bilirubin can show how serious the jaundice is and help decide the course of treatment. Tests to diagnose jaundice and measure bilirubin include: * A physical exam. * A laboratory test of a sample of your baby's blood. * A skin test with a device called a transcutaneous bilirubinometer, which measures the reflection of a special light shone through the skin. A healthcare professional may order additional tests if there's evidence that your baby's jaundice is caused by an underlying disorder. More Information Treatment Mild infant jaundice often disappears on its own within two or three weeks. For moderate or severe jaundice, a baby may need to stay longer in the newborn nursery or be readmitted to the hospital. Treatments to lower the level of bilirubin in baby's blood may include: * Light therapy, also called phototherapy. Your baby may be placed under a special lamp that emits light in the blue-green spectrum. The light changes the shape and structure of bilirubin molecules in such a way that they can be excreted in both the urine and stool. During treatment, your baby will wear only a diaper and protective eye patches. Light therapy may be supplemented with the use of a light-emitting pad or mattress. * Enhanced nutrition. To prevent weight loss, a healthcare professional may recommend more-frequent feeding or supplementation to ensure that your baby receives enough nutrition. * Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIg). Jaundice may be related to blood type differences between mother and baby. This condition results in the baby carrying antibodies from the mother that contribute to the rapid breakdown of the baby's red blood cells. Intravenous transfusion of an immunoglobulin — a blood protein that can reduce levels of antibodies — may decrease jaundice and lessen the need for an exchange transfusion, although results are not conclusive. * Exchange transfusion. Rarely, when severe jaundice doesn't respond to other treatments, a baby may need an exchange transfusion of blood. This involves repeatedly withdrawing small amounts of blood and replacing it with donor blood. The procedure dilutes the bilirubin and maternal antibodies and is done in a newborn intensive care unit. More Information Self care When infant jaundice isn't severe, a healthcare professional may recommend changes in feeding habits that can lower levels of bilirubin. Talk to your baby's healthcare professional if you have any questions or concerns about how much or how often your baby is feeding or if you're having trouble breastfeeding. The following steps may lessen jaundice: * More-frequent feedings. Feeding more frequently will provide your baby with more milk and cause more bowel movements, increasing the amount of bilirubin eliminated in your baby's stool. Infants who are breastfed should have 8 to 12 feedings a day for the first several days of life. Formula-fed infants usually should have 1 to 2 ounces (about 30 to 60 milliliters) of formula every 2 to 3 hours for the first week. * Supplemental feedings. If your baby is having trouble breastfeeding, is losing weight or is dehydrated, your baby's healthcare professional may suggest giving your baby formula or expressed milk to supplement breastfeeding. Depending on the situation, your baby's health professional may recommend using formula alone for a couple of days and then resuming breastfeeding. Ask your baby's health professional what feeding options are right for your baby. Preparing for your appointment Bilirubin levels in the blood tend to peak when a baby is between 2 and 5 days old. So it's important for your baby's healthcare professional to examine your baby for jaundice during that time. When your baby is discharged from the hospital, your baby will be checked for jaundice. If your baby has jaundice, your baby's healthcare professional will assess the likelihood of severe jaundice based on several factors: * How much bilirubin is in the blood. * Whether your baby was born prematurely. * How well your baby is feeding. * How old your baby is. * Whether your baby has bruising from delivery. * Whether an older sibling also had severe jaundice. Follow-up visit If risk factors for severe jaundice are present, your doctor may recommend a follow-up visit a day or two after the baby leaves the hospital. When you arrive for your follow-up appointment, be prepared to answer the following questions. * How well is your baby feeding? * Is your baby breastfed or formula-fed? * How often does your baby feed? * How often does your baby have a wet diaper? * How often is there stool in the diaper? * Does your baby wake up easily for feeding? * Does your baby seem sick or weak? * Have you noticed any changes in the color of your baby's skin or eyes? * If your baby has jaundice, has the yellow color spread to parts of the body other than the face? * Has your baby's temperature been stable? You also may prepare questions to ask your baby's care team at a follow-up appointment, including: * Is the jaundice severe? * What is the cause of the jaundice? * What tests does my baby need? * Does my baby need to begin treatment for jaundice? * Will my baby need to go back into the hospital? * When should my baby have a follow-up visit? * Should I keep feeding my baby the way I am now? * Can you recommend websites with information about jaundice? Do you have any brochures about jaundice and proper feeding?

fetched_contents.text: Growth of a Breastfed Baby Weight gain is a helpful measurement for determining how well your baby is doing. This is not the only way to know your baby is thriving, but it is a valuable indicator of health in a baby. If your baby is not gaining well, it can be a sign that breastfeeding is not going well. Or it may mean that a health issue is preventing your baby from growing as expected. There is a wide range of normal weight gain in babies. Many babies who gain weight slowly are perfectly healthy. It is important to look at all the signs of health when evaluating a baby’s growth pattern. Signs that Your Baby is Gaining Well * Your baby is waking up for feedings. * Your baby is alert and active during feedings. * Your baby is content after a feeding and has alert periods throughout the day. * Your baby has enough wet and poopy diapers each day for your baby’s age. See Poops and Pees for more information. * Your baby is gaining weight. * Your baby is reaching developmental milestones. For more information see How to Know Your Baby is Getting Enough Milk. Growth Charts In 2006 the World Health Organization (WHO) released new growth charts based on the feeding patterns of thousands of exclusively breastfed babies in six different countries (Brazil, Ghana, India, Norway, Oman and USA). In 2010, Dieticians of Canada, the Canadian Pediatric Society and others developed the WHO Growth Charts for Canada. These are the growth charts commonly used by Canadian healthcare providers. These charts contain five line graphs that indicate the expected growth curves for children from the smallest normally growing children (the 3rd percentile) to the largest normally growing children (the 97th percentile). A child who is in the 3rd percentile is smaller than 97 percent of babies the same age. A baby who is in the 97th percentile is smaller than only 3 percent of babies the same age. It doesn’t matter where your baby is on the growth chart. What is important is that your baby’s growth is relatively consistent on a curve. Benefits of newborn weight loss All babies lose weight initially after birth. This normal weight loss may help protect babies from obesity later in life. Two different studies revealed that babies who gained more than 100 g (3.5 oz) in the first week of life were significantly more likely to be overweight later in life. If you are only breastfeeding, your baby will start gaining weight by the second week. Unlike babies who are given formula, exclusively breastfed babies are less likely to gain too much weight in their first week of life. Impact of C-section vs. vaginal birth On average, babies born by a cesarean birth lose more weight than babies born vaginally. Exclusively breastfed babies born by a vaginal birth have a median weight loss of 7.1%. Those born by a cesarean birth have a median weight loss of 8.6%. They also lose more weight for a longer period of time (more than 72 hours) than exclusively breastfed babies born vaginally (between 48 and 72 hours). This is perhaps because the medications used in labour (epidurals and narcotics) can remain in the baby’s system for up to a week. This can make your baby sleepy and nursing more difficult in the early days. Impact of IV fluids in labor Several studies have found that the larger the volume of IV fluids a mother receives during labour, the more weight her baby loses in the first 24 hours. This is because the IV fluids pass to the baby’s body and increase the baby’s birth weight. In the first 24 hours after birth babies, whose mothers received IV fluids during labour, produce more wet diapers than babies, whose mothers do not receive IV fluids. The extra wet diapers result in an extra weight loss. This weight loss is completely unrelated to how much colostrum the baby drinks in the first 24 hours. If you have received IV fluids during labour, it is recommended that you measure your baby’s weight 24 hours after birth. At this time, most of the excess water will have been peed out. This 24-hour weight can be used to measure your baby’s future weight loss more accurately than the inflated birth weight. Other factors that influence birth weight Canadian researchers found that the following factors can influence weight loss: * Heavier babies lose more weight. * Babies born earlier than 40 weeks lose more weight. * Baby girls lose more weight than baby boys. Impact of gestational diabetes on weight gain in the first few days If you have gestational diabetes, your milk may come in a day or two later than expected. This can lead to greater weight loss in your baby in the first week. You can prepare for this possibility by expressing your colostrum during pregnancy. Bring it with you to the birth and feed it to your baby, if needed. Prenatal colostrum expression Most women with low-risk pregnancies can begin hand expression at 37 weeks. Consult your healthcare provider if you have any concerns. This colostrum can be stored in small syringes or small glass jars in your freezer. If your baby loses more weight than normal in the first couple of days, your stored colostrum can be given to your baby by cup or syringe after nursing. The volumes of colostrum in the early days are too small to give with a bottle. See Prenatal Colostrum Expression for more information. Reasons for concern in the early days Weight loss of more than 10% is reason for concern. If this is the case, your baby should be examined by a doctor for signs of dehydration. Positioning, latching and breastfeeding management also need to be evaluated, ideally by an International Board Certified Lactation Consultant (IBCLC). Supplementation may be required if there is significant weight loss and/or if nursing is not going well. Dehydration can lead to serious health problems. In most situations, the reason for excessive weight loss is poor positioning and latching. This can result in your baby not getting enough milk. fetched_contents.text: Sepsis in the Newborn Not what you're looking for? What is newborn sepsis? Newborn sepsis is a severe infection in an infant younger than 28 days old. The infection is in your baby’s blood. But it may affect any body system or the whole body. What causes newborn sepsis? Newborn sepsis is most often caused by bacteria. But other germs can also cause it. A baby may become infected before birth if your amniotic fluid is infected. During delivery, the newborn may be exposed to germs in the birth canal. Once born, a baby may be exposed to germs in the hospital or at home. Which babies are at risk for newborn sepsis? These things make it more likely that your newborn will have sepsis: * Your baby is born too early (premature). This means before 37 weeks of pregnancy. * Your amniotic sac breaks (ruptures) more than 18 hours before birth. * You have the strep germ in your vagina or have symptoms of infected amniotic fluid, such as a fever. * Your baby needs a medical procedure. This includes a urinary catheter or a central IV (intravenous) line. What are the symptoms of newborn sepsis? Sepsis in newborns can be hard to identify. Symptoms depend on what’s causing the infection. They also depend on how severe the infection is and where it is. The newborn may have: * Signs of distress during labor or delivery, such as a rapid heart rate * Changes in temperature (often fever) * Breathing problems, such as very fast breathing and grunting * Digestive problems like poor appetite or an enlarged liver * Nervous system problems, such as drowsiness or trouble staying awake * Irritability How is newborn sepsis diagnosed? The symptoms of sepsis are similar to some other health conditions. Your baby will need tests to make a sepsis diagnosis and to rule out other illnesses. These tests may include: * Blood culture. This is done to check for bacteria in the blood. Results take a few days, but treatment will start right away. This is the main way sepsis is diagnosed. * Urine culture. This checks for bacteria in the urinary system. * Other cultures. This checks for bacteria in other places, such as in a wound. * Blood tests. These check for signs of infection. They also check for possible effects of sepsis on the kidneys, liver, and blood cells. * Lumbar puncture. This is done to check for infection of the brain and spinal cord (meningitis). A small amount of cerebrospinal fluid is tested. * X-rays or other imaging tests. For example, a chest X-ray is used to check for a lung infection. How is newborn sepsis treated? Treatment will depend on your baby’s symptoms, age, and general health. It will also depend on how severe the condition is. Early diagnosis and treatment is the best way to stop sepsis. If your baby’s healthcare provider thinks it may be sepsis, your baby will get antibiotics right away, even before test results are available. Once the provider has the test results, they may change the treatment. A newborn with sepsis may be very ill. The baby will need to stay in the newborn intensive care unit (NICU). In the NICU, your baby will be watched very closely. In addition to the antibiotics, they will get fluids, other medicines, oxygen, nutrition, and help with breathing, if needed. What are possible complications of newborn sepsis? Sepsis is life-threatening for newborns. It can affect any body system. It often affects more than 1 system at the same time. Can newborn sepsis be prevented? Newborn sepsis can’t be completely prevented. But you can lower the risk. Regular prenatal care can find and treat many problems that put a newborn at risk for sepsis. One example of this is that all pregnant women are screened for group B strep infection and treated if they have it. Hospitals and other facilities have practices in place to prevent the spread of infection. These include: * Frequent handwashing * Limiting procedures that include making cuts or putting tools into the body When should I call my baby’s healthcare provider? Call your baby’s healthcare provider right away if your newborn has: * A fever above 100.4°F (38.0°C) rectally * A fever lasting more than 1 day * Trouble breathing * A change in behavior, such as being very sleepy, fussy, or not eating well Key points about newborn sepsis * Newborn sepsis is a severe infection in an infant younger than 28 days old. * A newborn may become infected before, during, or after birth. * Newborn sepsis can be hard to diagnose. * Early diagnosis and treatment are the best ways to stop sepsis. * Antibiotic medicine is started as soon as possible. Next steps Tips to help you get the most from a visit to your child’s healthcare provider: * Know the reason for the visit and what you want to happen. * Before your visit, write down questions you want answered. * At the visit, write down the name of a new diagnosis and any new medicines, treatments, or tests. Also write down any new instructions your provider gives you for your child. * Know why a new medicine or treatment is prescribed and how it will help your child. Also know what the side effects are and when they should be reported. * Ask if your child’s condition can be treated in other ways. * Know why a test or procedure is recommended and what the results could mean. * Know what to expect if your child does not take the medicine or have the test or procedure. * If your child has a follow-up appointment, write down the date, time, and purpose for that visit. * Know how you can contact your child’s provider after office hours, and on weekends and holidays. This is important if your child becomes ill and you have questions or need advice. ## Differential diagnosis and urgency assessment for a 6-day-old full-term newborn

### Most likely conditions in a 6-day-old full-term newborn
In a 6-day-old full-term newborn, the most likely conditions are **jaundice**, **feeding difficulties**, and **infection/sepsis**, with **apnea** being less common but still relevant in certain clinical contexts. The evidence consistently identifies jaundice as extremely common in newborns, with about six out of 10 newborns having jaundice to varying degrees [N1-R2]. Neonatal jaundice is described as yellow coloring of the skin and eyes due to bilirubin buildup [N1-R1], and it is a leading reason for concern at this age [N1-R3]. Feeding problems are also common in newborns, especially in breastfed infants, and poor feeding can overlap with jaundice and infection [N1-R4][N3-R5]. Neonatal sepsis is another critical possibility, especially because newborns can develop signs rapidly and the infection may affect multiple body systems [N4-R1][N4-F3].

### Red flags that require immediate care
The red flags that require immediate care are the most serious signs of infection or severe disease. These include:
- **Fever or very low temperature** [N4-R2][N4-F3]
- **Poor feeding or refusing to eat** [N4-R2][N4-F3]
- **Unusual sleepiness or difficulty waking** [N4-R2][N4-F3]
- **Abnormal breathing or respiratory distress** [N4-R1][N4-F3]
- **Changes in behavior, such as being very sleepy, fussy, or not eating well** [N4-F3]
- **Changes in skin color or jaundice spreading beyond the face** [N2-F1]
- **Dehydration signs** [N3-F2]
- **Lethargy, irritability, or poor feeding** [N1-R3][N4-R1]

These signs are particularly urgent because they may indicate **neonatal sepsis**, **severe hyperbilirubinemia**, or other serious conditions requiring prompt evaluation [N4-F3][N1-R3]. The evidence also notes that jaundice should be assessed for clinical features of bilirubin encephalopathy, including poor feeding and lethargy, which are red flags for urgent jaundice management [N1-R3].

### When to suspect jaundice, infection, apnea, or feeding problems
- **Jaundice** should be suspected when the baby’s skin and eyes appear yellow, especially after the first few days of life, when bilirubin levels peak [N1-R1][N2-F1]. The Mayo Clinic emphasizes that jaundice is common and that bilirubin levels should be measured to determine how serious it is [N2-F1].
- **Infection/sepsis** should be suspected when there is fever, low temperature, poor feeding, lethargy, or other signs of systemic illness [N4-R1][N4-F3]. The evidence also states that newborn sepsis can be hard to diagnose and may present with fever, changes in temperature, breathing problems, or digestive issues [N4-F3].
- **Apnea** should be suspected in a newborn who stops breathing, especially if there are episodes of apnea or respiratory distress [N5-R3][N5-R4]. The evidence suggests that CPAP is used for apnea in preterm neonates when the infant continues to have apneic episodes, and CPAP is used to provide respiratory support for neonates with upper airway obstruction or respiratory failure [N5-R3][N5-R4].
- **Feeding problems** should be suspected when the baby is not feeding well, is losing weight, is dehydrated, or is not waking for feedings [N3-F2][N3-R5]. Breastfeeding support and feeding frequency are strongly linked to jaundice and feeding outcomes [N7-R2][N7-R5].

### How feeding issues may overlap with jaundice or infection
Feeding issues may overlap with jaundice because poor feeding can reduce stool output and delay bilirubin excretion, which worsens jaundice [N1-R4][N3-F2]. The evidence also notes that breastfeeding does not cause jaundice, but poor feeding and not getting enough breast milk are risk factors for high bilirubin levels [N7-R5]. Feeding issues may also overlap with infection because poor feeding can be a sign of systemic illness or sepsis, and infection can itself impair feeding and weight gain [N4-F3][N3-R5]. In short, feeding problems are not isolated; they can reflect bilirubin-related physiology, infection, or inadequate nutrition [N1-R4][N4-F3][N7-R5].

## Management and next steps for each concern

### Feeding support and hydration strategies
Feeding support should be individualized, with frequent feeding and hydration as the mainstays. For breastfed infants, the evidence strongly supports frequent breastfeeding, with 8 to 12 feedings a day for the first several days of life [N2-F1]. For formula-fed infants, the evidence recommends 1 to 2 ounces every 2 to 3 hours for the first week [N2-F1]. Poor feeding can also be managed with **supplemental feeding** if the baby is losing weight, dehydrated, or not feeding well [N2-F1]. The La Leche League Canada source emphasizes that scheduled feedings, swaddling, and pacifiers can reduce feeding cues, so feeding support should also focus on positioning, latching, and breastfeeding management [N3-F2]. If there is significant weight loss, positioning and latching need evaluation by an IBCLC, and supplementation may be required [N3-F2].

### Jaundice monitoring and treatment options
Jaundice should be monitored by assessing bilirubin levels and watching for progression of yellowing beyond the face [N2-F1]. The evidence states that jaundice often disappears on its own within two to three weeks, but moderate or severe jaundice may require prolonged hospital stay or readmission [N2-F1]. Treatment options include:
- **Phototherapy**, which is described as safe and effective for decreasing unconjugated bilirubin and reducing the need for exchange transfusion [N2-R3]. Mayo Clinic notes that phototherapy may be supplemented with light-emitting pads or mattresses [N2-R5].
- **Enhanced nutrition**, including more frequent feedings and supplemental feeding, to increase stool output and bilirubin excretion [N2-F1].
- **Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIg)** may be considered if jaundice is related to blood type differences, although results are not conclusive [N2-F1].
- **Exchange transfusion** is reserved for severe jaundice that does not respond to other treatments [N2-F1].

The evidence also notes that jaundice can be mild and self-limited, but bilirubin levels should guide treatment decisions [N2-F1].

### Infection and apnea workup and management
For infection, the workup should be prompt and includes blood culture, urine culture, and other cultures if needed, plus blood tests, lumbar puncture, and imaging if indicated [N4-F3]. The evidence states that newborn sepsis is diagnosed with blood culture as the main method, and treatment should start immediately with antibiotics even before test results are available [N4-F3]. The baby may need to stay in the NICU for close monitoring and supportive care, including fluids, oxygen, nutrition, and help with breathing [N4-F3].

For **apnea**, the evidence suggests that CPAP is used for apnea in preterm neonates when the infant continues to have apneic episodes [N5-R3]. CPAP is also described as a means of providing respiratory support for neonates with upper airway obstruction or respiratory failure [N5-R4]. The evidence also notes that CPAP has been shown to be relatively safe and effective in preventing and treating respiratory distress among preterm infants [N5-R1]. For apnea management, the workup would likely include respiratory assessment, oxygenation, and evaluation of underlying causes such as prematurity or airway obstruction.

### When to use phototherapy, CPAP, or supplemental feeding
- **Phototherapy** is used when jaundice is moderate or severe and bilirubin levels are high enough to require intervention [N2-F1]. The Mayo Clinic states that phototherapy should be instituted when the total serum bilirubin is at or above 15 mg/dL in infants 25 to 48 hours old [N2-R2]. The evidence also emphasizes that phototherapy is often the preferred treatment for neonatal hyperbilirubinemia [N2-R1].
- **CPAP** is used for apnea or respiratory support in neonates with upper airway obstruction or respiratory failure, especially when apnea persists [N5-R3][N5-R4]. It is also used in postextubation respiratory support [N5-R5].
- **Supplemental feeding** is used when the baby is not feeding well, is losing weight, is dehydrated, or when more nutrition is needed to support bilirubin excretion and growth [N2-F1][N3-F2]. The evidence recommends more-frequent feedings, supplementation, or formula feeding if breastfeeding is not sufficient [N2-F1].

In summary, management should be guided by the severity of the condition: phototherapy for jaundice, CPAP for apnea or respiratory support, and supplemental feeding or enhanced nutrition for feeding problems [N2-R3][N5-R3][N2-F1].

## Family reassurance and practical guidance

### What parents should watch for at home
Parents should watch for signs that may indicate a problem, including:
- **Jaundice**, especially if the yellow color spreads beyond the face [N2-F1]
- **Poor feeding** or feeding difficulty [N3-F2]
- **Weight loss that is too much or too slow** [N3-F2]
- **Changes in behavior**, such as being very sleepy, fussy, or not eating well [N4-F3]
- **Fever or very low temperature** [N4-F3]
- **Abnormal breathing** or signs of respiratory distress [N4-F3]
- **Dehydration**, including fewer wet or poopy diapers than expected [N3-F2]
- **Lethargy, irritability, or poor feeding** [N1-R3][N4-R1]
- **Any unusual changes in the baby’s appearance, activity level, or alertness** [N2-F1]

The evidence emphasizes that jaundice can be mild and self-limited, but it still needs careful monitoring because it can progress [N2-F1]. Parents should also be alert for signs of infection, as these can develop rapidly and may not always be obvious [N4-F3].

### When to call the doctor or return for care
Parents should call the doctor or return for care if the baby:
- Has **jaundice spreading beyond the face** [N2-F1]
- Is **not feeding well** [N3-F2]
- Has **poor feeding or refuses to eat** [N4-F3]
- Has **fever or very low temperature** [N4-F3]
- Has **abnormal breathing** or signs of respiratory distress [N4-F3]
- Has **unusual sleepiness, fussy behavior, or difficulty waking** [N4-F3]
- Has **changes in behavior** that suggest illness [N4-F3]
- Has **dehydration** signs [N3-F2]
- Has **weight loss greater than 10%** [N3-F2]
- Has **any other red flags** that make the parents concerned [N4-F3]

The evidence also states that if the baby’s healthcare provider thinks sepsis may be present, antibiotics are started immediately and the baby is often admitted to the NICU [N4-F3]. Parents should act quickly if any of these signs appear.

### Routine follow-up and developmental expectations
Routine follow-up is important for a 6-day-old full-term newborn. The evidence states that newborn care guidelines recommend a postdischarge assessment within the first week of life, with most guidelines recommending follow-up within 48 hours after discharge or 3 to 5 days after birth [N6-R2][N6-R3]. The evidence also notes that newborns discharged before 48 hours should generally have follow-up within 48 hours after discharge [N6-R1]. Follow-up should include checking feeding, weight gain, wet and poopy diapers, and any signs of jaundice or infection [N2-F1][N3-F2].

Developmentally, the evidence emphasizes that weight gain is a helpful but not the only indicator of health, and that many babies who gain weight slowly are still healthy [N3-F2]. It also notes that babies who are not gaining well may have breastfeeding problems or a health issue, and that growth should be consistent on a growth curve [N3-F2]. Parents should be reassured that babies can lose weight initially after birth, and that this is normal unless it is excessive [N3-F2].

### How to recognize jaundice and feeding concerns
To recognize **jaundice**, parents should look for yellowing of the skin and eyes, especially beyond the face, and note whether the jaundice is worsening over time [N2-F1]. The Mayo Clinic advises that bilirubin levels should be measured to determine how serious jaundice is [N2-F1].

To recognize **feeding concerns**, parents should watch for:
- **Poor feeding or feeding difficulty** [N3-F2]
- **Weight loss** or slow weight gain [N3-F2]
- **Few wet or poopy diapers** than expected for the baby’s age [N3-F2]
- **Lethargy, irritability, or poor alertness** during feedings [N3-F2]
- **Not waking for feedings** [N3-F2]

The evidence also states that frequent and effective breastfeeding helps the baby eliminate bilirubin and that poor feeding and not getting enough milk are risk factors for high bilirubin levels [N7-R2][N7-R5]. Breastfeeding support and feeding frequency are therefore central to recognizing and managing feeding concerns [N7-R2][N7-R5].

# Integrated patient-facing answer for a 6-day-old full-term boy

## What the doctor needs to know
A 6-day-old full-term boy with a normal birth at 39 weeks is likely to be healthy, but there are several important concerns that may arise around this age. The most likely problems are **jaundice**, **feeding difficulties**, and **infection or sepsis**, with **apnea** being less common but still relevant in some cases [N8]. The evidence shows that jaundice is very common in newborns, with about six out of 10 newborns having jaundice to varying degrees [N1-R2], and that feeding problems can overlap with jaundice or infection [N8]. The main red flags that require immediate care are fever or very low temperature, poor feeding or refusal to eat, unusual sleepiness or difficulty waking, abnormal breathing, and changes in behavior such as being very sleepy, fussy, or not eating well [N8].

## Most likely conditions in a 6-day-old full-term newborn
### 1. Jaundice
Jaundice is the most common concern at this age. It is described as yellow coloring of the skin and eyes due to bilirubin buildup, and it is very common in newborns [N1-R1][N1-R2]. The evidence also states that jaundice should be assessed for clinical features of bilirubin encephalopathy, including poor feeding and lethargy [N1-R3]. Jaundice is not always serious, but it does require monitoring because bilirubin levels can rise and may need treatment [N2-F1].

### 2. Feeding difficulties
Feeding problems are also common, especially in breastfed newborns. Poor feeding can reduce stool output and delay bilirubin excretion, which can worsen jaundice [N1-R4][N3-F2]. The evidence also notes that poor feeding and not getting enough breast milk are risk factors for high bilirubin levels [N7-R5]. If the baby is not feeding well, losing weight, or is dehydrated, that is a sign that feeding support may be needed [N3-F2].

### 3. Infection or sepsis
Newborn sepsis is another serious possibility. The evidence says that neonatal sepsis can be hard to diagnose and may present with fever, changes in temperature, breathing problems, or digestive issues [N4-F3]. It can also cause poor feeding, lethargy, and unusual sleepiness [N4-R2][N4-F3]. The evidence emphasizes that sepsis is life-threatening and that early diagnosis and treatment are the best ways to stop it [N4-F3].

### 4. Apnea
Apnea is less common in full-term newborns than in preterm infants, but it can still occur and should be evaluated if the baby stops breathing or has episodes of apnea [N5-R3]. The evidence indicates that CPAP is used for apnea in preterm neonates when the infant continues to have apneic episodes, and that CPAP is used as respiratory support for neonates with upper airway obstruction or respiratory failure [N5-R3][N5-R4].

## When to suspect jaundice, infection, apnea, or feeding problems
### Jaundice
Suspect jaundice if the baby’s skin and eyes appear yellow, especially after the first few days of life when bilirubin levels peak [N1-R1][N2-F1]. The evidence also states that jaundice is often mild and self-limited, but bilirubin levels should be measured to determine how serious it is [N2-F1].

### Infection
Suspect infection if there is fever, very low temperature, poor feeding, lethargy, unusual sleepiness, or any signs of systemic illness [N4-R2][N4-F3]. The evidence also notes that newborn sepsis can present with fever, changes in temperature, breathing problems, or digestive issues [N4-F3].

### Apnea
Suspect apnea if the baby stops breathing or has episodes of apnea, especially if there are signs of respiratory distress [N5-R3]. CPAP is used when apnea persists and when respiratory support is needed [N5-R3][N5-R4].

### Feeding problems
Suspect feeding problems if the baby is not feeding well, is losing weight, is dehydrated, or is not waking for feedings [N3-F2][N3-R5]. The evidence also notes that poor feeding can be a sign of systemic illness or sepsis [N4-F3].

## How feeding issues may overlap with jaundice or infection
Feeding issues can overlap with jaundice because poor feeding can reduce stool output and delay bilirubin excretion, which worsens jaundice [N1-R4][N3-F2]. The evidence also states that breastfeeding does not cause jaundice, but poor feeding and not getting enough breast milk are risk factors for high bilirubin levels [N7-R5]. Feeding issues can also overlap with infection because poor feeding can be a sign of systemic illness or sepsis, and infection can itself impair feeding and weight gain [N4-F3][N3-R5]. In short, feeding problems are not isolated; they can reflect bilirubin-related physiology, infection, or inadequate nutrition [N1-R4][N4-F3][N7-R5].

## What parents should watch for at home
Parents should watch for the following signs at home:
- **Jaundice**, especially if the yellow color spreads beyond the face [N2-F1]
- **Poor feeding** or feeding difficulty [N3-F2]
- **Weight loss that is too much or too slow** [N3-F2]
- **Changes in behavior**, such as being very sleepy, fussy, or not eating well [N4-F3]
- **Fever or very low temperature** [N4-F3]
- **Abnormal breathing** or signs of respiratory distress [N4-F3]
- **Dehydration**, including fewer wet or poopy diapers than expected [N3-F2]
- **Lethargy, irritability, or poor feeding** [N1-R3][N4-R1]

The evidence emphasizes that jaundice can be mild and self-limited, but it still needs careful monitoring because it can progress [N2-F1]. Parents should also be alert for signs of infection, as these can develop rapidly and may not always be obvious [N4-F3].

## When to call the doctor or return for care
Parents should call the doctor or return for care if the baby:
- Has **jaundice spreading beyond the face** [N2-F1]
- Is **not feeding well** [N3-F2]
- Has **poor feeding or refuses to eat** [N4-F3]
- Has **fever or very low temperature** [N4-F3]
- Has **abnormal breathing** or signs of respiratory distress [N4-F3]
- Has **unusual sleepiness, fussy behavior, or difficulty waking** [N4-F3]
- Has **changes in behavior** that suggest illness [N4-F3]
- Has **dehydration** signs [N3-F2]
- Has **weight loss greater than 10%** [N3-F2]
- Has **any other red flags** that make the parents concerned [N4-F3]

The evidence also states that if the baby’s healthcare provider thinks sepsis may be present, antibiotics are started immediately and the baby is often admitted to the NICU [N4-F3]. Parents should act quickly if any of these signs appear.

## Routine follow-up and developmental expectations
Routine follow-up is important for a 6-day-old full-term newborn. The evidence states that newborn care guidelines recommend a postdischarge assessment within the first week of life, with most guidelines recommending follow-up within 48 hours after discharge or 3 to 5 days after birth [N6-R2][N6-R3]. The evidence also notes that newborns discharged before 48 hours should generally have follow-up within 48 hours after discharge [N6-R1]. Follow-up should include checking feeding, weight gain, wet and poopy diapers, and any signs of jaundice or infection [N2-F1][N3-F2].

Developmentally, the evidence emphasizes that weight gain is a helpful but not the only indicator of health, and that many babies who gain weight slowly are still healthy [N3-F2]. It also notes that babies who are not gaining well may have breastfeeding problems or a health issue, and that growth should be consistent on a growth curve [N3-F2]. Parents should be reassured that babies can lose weight initially after birth, and that this is normal unless it is excessive [N3-F2].

## How to recognize jaundice and feeding concerns
### Jaundice
To recognize jaundice, look for yellowing of the skin and eyes, especially beyond the face [N2-F1]. The Mayo Clinic advises that bilirubin levels should be measured to determine how serious jaundice is [N2-F1].

### Feeding concerns
To recognize feeding concerns, watch for:
- **Poor feeding or feeding difficulty** [N3-F2]
- **Weight loss** or slow weight gain [N3-F2]
- **Few wet or poopy diapers** than expected for the baby’s age [N3-F2]
- **Lethargy, irritability, or poor alertness** during feedings [N3-F2]
- **Not waking for feedings** [N3-F2]

The evidence also states that frequent and effective breastfeeding helps the baby eliminate bilirubin and that poor feeding and not getting enough milk are risk factors for high bilirubin levels [N7-R2][N7-R5]. Breastfeeding support and feeding frequency are therefore central to recognizing and managing feeding concerns [N7-R2][N7-R5].

## Management and next steps
### Feeding support and hydration strategies
Feeding support should be individualized, with frequent feeding and hydration as the mainstays. For breastfed infants, the evidence strongly supports frequent breastfeeding, with 8 to 12 feedings a day for the first several days of life [N2-F1]. For formula-fed infants, the evidence recommends 1 to 2 ounces every 2 to 3 hours for the first week [N2-F1]. Poor feeding can also be managed with **supplemental feeding** if the baby is losing weight, dehydrated, or not feeding well [N2-F1]. The La Leche League Canada source emphasizes that scheduled feedings, swaddling, and pacifiers can reduce feeding cues, so feeding support should also focus on positioning, latching, and breastfeeding management [N3-F2]. If there is significant weight loss, positioning and latching need evaluation by an IBCLC, and supplementation may be required [N3-F2].

### Jaundice monitoring and treatment options
Jaundice should be monitored by assessing bilirubin levels and watching for progression of yellowing beyond the face [N2-F1]. The evidence states that jaundice often disappears on its own within two to three weeks, but moderate or severe jaundice may require prolonged hospital stay or readmission [N2-F1]. Treatment options include:
- **Phototherapy**, which is described as safe and effective for decreasing unconjugated bilirubin and reducing the need for exchange transfusion [N2-R3]. Mayo Clinic notes that phototherapy may be supplemented with light-emitting pads or mattresses [N2-R5].
- **Enhanced nutrition**, including more frequent feedings and supplemental feeding, to increase stool output and bilirubin excretion [N2-F1].
- **Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIg)** may be considered if jaundice is related to blood type differences, although results are not conclusive [N2-F1].
- **Exchange transfusion** is reserved for severe jaundice that does not respond to other treatments [N2-F1].

The evidence also notes that jaundice can be mild and self-limited, but bilirubin levels should guide treatment decisions [N2-F1].

### Infection and apnea workup and management
For infection, the workup should be prompt and includes blood culture, urine culture, and other cultures if needed, plus blood tests, lumbar puncture, and imaging if indicated [N4-F3]. The evidence states that newborn sepsis is diagnosed with blood culture as the main method, and treatment should start immediately with antibiotics even before test results are available [N4-F3]. The baby may need to stay in the NICU for close monitoring and supportive care, including fluids, oxygen, nutrition, and help with breathing [N4-F3].

For **apnea**, the evidence suggests that CPAP is used for apnea in preterm neonates when the infant continues to have apneic episodes [N5-R3]. CPAP is also described as a means of providing respiratory support for neonates with upper airway obstruction or respiratory failure [N5-R4]. The evidence also notes that CPAP has been shown to be relatively safe and effective in preventing and treating respiratory distress among preterm infants [N5-R1]. For apnea management, the workup would likely include respiratory assessment, oxygenation, and evaluation of underlying causes such as prematurity or airway obstruction.

### When to use phototherapy, CPAP, or supplemental feeding
- **Phototherapy** is used when jaundice is moderate or severe and bilirubin levels are high enough to require intervention [N2-F1]. The Mayo Clinic states that phototherapy should be instituted when the total serum bilirubin is at or above 15 mg/dL in infants 25 to 48 hours old [N2-R2]. The evidence also emphasizes that phototherapy is often the preferred treatment for neonatal hyperbilirubinemia [N2-R1].
- **CPAP** is used for apnea or respiratory support in neonates with upper airway obstruction or respiratory failure, especially when apnea persists [N5-R3][N5-R4]. It is also used in postextubation respiratory support [N5-R5].
- **Supplemental feeding** is used when the baby is not feeding well, is losing weight, is dehydrated, or when more nutrition is needed to support bilirubin excretion and growth [N2-F1][N3-F2]. The evidence recommends more-frequent feedings, supplementation, or formula feeding if breastfeeding is not sufficient [N2-F1].

## Bottom line for parents
In short, a 6-day-old full-term newborn is likely to be healthy, but parents should watch for jaundice, feeding problems, infection, or apnea. Jaundice is common but usually mild and self-limited; feeding problems can overlap with jaundice or infection; and infection or sepsis can develop rapidly with fever, poor feeding, or unusual behavior [N8][N9]. If any red flags appear, parents should call the doctor or return for care immediately [N8][N9]. Routine follow-up is important, and most babies do well with frequent feeding, consistent weight gain, and prompt attention to any changes [N10].

## Differential diagnosis and urgency assessment for a 6-day-old full-term newborn

### Most likely conditions in a 6-day-old full-term newborn
In a 6-day-old full-term newborn, the most likely conditions are **jaundice**, **feeding difficulties**, and **infection/sepsis**, with **apnea** being less common but still relevant in certain clinical contexts. The evidence consistently identifies jaundice as extremely common in newborns, with about six out of 10 newborns having jaundice to varying degrees [N1-R2]. Neonatal jaundice is described as yellow coloring of the skin and eyes due to bilirubin buildup [N1-R1], and it is a leading reason for concern at this age [N1-R3]. Feeding problems are also common in newborns, especially in breastfed infants, and poor feeding can overlap with jaundice and infection [N1-R4][N3-R5]. Neonatal sepsis is another critical possibility, especially because newborns can develop signs rapidly and the infection may affect multiple body systems [N4-R1][N4-F3].

### Red flags that require immediate care
The red flags that require immediate care are the most serious signs of infection or severe disease. These include:
- **Fever or very low temperature** [N4-R2][N4-F3]
- **Poor feeding or refusing to eat** [N4-R2][N4-F3]
- **Unusual sleepiness or difficulty waking** [N4-R2][N4-F3]
- **Abnormal breathing or respiratory distress** [N4-R1][N4-F3]
- **Changes in behavior, such as being very sleepy, fussy, or not eating well** [N4-F3]
- **Changes in skin color or jaundice spreading beyond the face** [N2-F1]
- **Dehydration signs** [N3-F2]
- **Lethargy, irritability, or poor feeding** [N1-R3][N4-R1]

These signs are particularly urgent because they may indicate **neonatal sepsis**, **severe hyperbilirubinemia**, or other serious conditions requiring prompt evaluation [N4-F3][N1-R3]. The evidence also notes that jaundice should be assessed for clinical features of bilirubin encephalopathy, including poor feeding and lethargy, which are red flags for urgent jaundice management [N1-R3].

### When to suspect jaundice, infection, apnea, or feeding problems
- **Jaundice** should be suspected when the baby’s skin and eyes appear yellow, especially after the first few days of life, when bilirubin levels peak [N1-R1][N2-F1]. The Mayo Clinic emphasizes that jaundice is common and that bilirubin levels should be measured to determine how serious it is [N2-F1].
- **Infection/sepsis** should be suspected when there is fever, low temperature, poor feeding, lethargy, or other signs of systemic illness [N4-R1][N4-F3]. The evidence also states that newborn sepsis can be hard to diagnose and may present with fever, changes in temperature, breathing problems, or digestive issues [N4-F3].
- **Apnea** should be suspected in a newborn who stops breathing, especially if there are episodes of apnea or respiratory distress [N5-R3][N5-R4]. The evidence suggests that CPAP is used for apnea in preterm neonates when the infant continues to have apneic episodes, and CPAP is used to provide respiratory support for neonates with upper airway obstruction or respiratory failure [N5-R3][N5-R4].
- **Feeding problems** should be suspected when the baby is not feeding well, is losing weight, is dehydrated, or is not waking for feedings [N3-F2][N3-R5]. Breastfeeding support and feeding frequency are strongly linked to jaundice and feeding outcomes [N7-R2][N7-R5].

### How feeding issues may overlap with jaundice or infection
Feeding issues may overlap with jaundice because poor feeding can reduce stool output and delay bilirubin excretion, which worsens jaundice [N1-R4][N3-F2]. The evidence also notes that breastfeeding does not cause jaundice, but poor feeding and not getting enough breast milk are risk factors for high bilirubin levels [N7-R5]. Feeding issues may also overlap with infection because poor feeding can be a sign of systemic illness or sepsis, and infection can itself impair feeding and weight gain [N4-F3][N3-R5]. In short, feeding problems are not isolated; they can reflect bilirubin-related physiology, infection, or inadequate nutrition [N1-R4][N4-F3][N7-R5].

A 6-day-old full-term boy with a normal birth at 39 weeks is likely to be healthy, but there are several important concerns that may arise around this age. The main red flags that require immediate care are fever or very low temperature, poor feeding or refusal to eat, unusual sleepiness or difficulty waking, abnormal breathing, and changes in behavior such as being very sleepy, fussy, or not eating well [N8].

## Most likely conditions in a 6-day-old full-term newborn
### 1. Jaundice
Jaundice is the most common concern at this age. It is described as yellow coloring of the skin and eyes due to bilirubin buildup, and it is very common in newborns [N1-R1][N1-R2]. The evidence also states that jaundice should be assessed for clinical features of bilirubin encephalopathy, including poor feeding and lethargy [N1-R3]. Jaundice is not always serious, but it does require monitoring because bilirubin levels can rise and may need treatment [N2-F1].

### 2. Feeding difficulties
Feeding problems are also common, especially in breastfed newborns. Poor feeding can reduce stool output and delay bilirubin excretion, which can worsen jaundice [N1-R4][N3-F2]. The evidence also notes that poor feeding and not getting enough breast milk are risk factors for high bilirubin levels [N7-R5]. If the baby is not feeding well, losing weight, or is dehydrated, that is a sign that feeding support may be needed [N3-F2].

### 3. Infection or sepsis
Newborn sepsis is another serious possibility. The evidence says that neonatal sepsis can be hard to diagnose and may present with fever, changes in temperature, breathing problems, or digestive issues [N4-F3]. It can also cause poor feeding, lethargy, and unusual sleepiness [N4-R2][N4-F3]. The evidence emphasizes that sepsis is life-threatening and that early diagnosis and treatment are the best ways to stop it [N4-F3].

Apnea is less common in full-term newborns than in preterm infants, but it can still occur and should be evaluated if the baby stops breathing or has episodes of apnea [N5-R3]. ### Feeding problems

- Is **not feeding well** [N3-F2]

### Jaundice
To recognize jaundice, look for yellowing of the skin and eyes, especially beyond the face [N2-F1]. The Mayo Clinic advises that bilirubin levels should be measured to determine how serious jaundice is [N2-F1].

- **Poor feeding or feeding difficulty** [N3-F2]
- **Weight loss** or slow weight gain [N3-F2]
- **Few wet or poopy diapers** than expected for the baby’s age [N3-F2]
- **Lethargy, irritability, or poor alertness** during feedings [N3-F2]
- **Not waking for feedings** [N3-F2]

Breastfeeding support and feeding frequency are therefore central to recognizing and managing feeding concerns [N7-R2][N7-R5].

## Management and next steps
### Feeding support and hydration strategies
Feeding support should be individualized, with frequent feeding and hydration as the mainstays. For breastfed infants, the evidence strongly supports frequent breastfeeding, with 8 to 12 feedings a day for the first several days of life [N2-F1]. For formula-fed infants, the evidence recommends 1 to 2 ounces every 2 to 3 hours for the first week [N2-F1]. Poor feeding can also be managed with **supplemental feeding** if the baby is losing weight, dehydrated, or not feeding well [N2-F1]. The La Leche League Canada source emphasizes that scheduled feedings, swaddling, and pacifiers can reduce feeding cues, so feeding support should also focus on positioning, latching, and breastfeeding management [N3-F2]. If there is significant weight loss, positioning and latching need evaluation by an IBCLC, and supplementation may be required [N3-F2].

### Jaundice monitoring and treatment options
Jaundice should be monitored by assessing bilirubin levels and watching for progression of yellowing beyond the face [N2-F1]. The evidence states that jaundice often disappears on its own within two to three weeks, but moderate or severe jaundice may require prolonged hospital stay or readmission [N2-F1]. Treatment options include:
- **Phototherapy**, which is described as safe and effective for decreasing unconjugated bilirubin and reducing the need for exchange transfusion [N2-R3]. Mayo Clinic notes that phototherapy may be supplemented with light-emitting pads or mattresses [N2-R5].
- **Enhanced nutrition**, including more frequent feedings and supplemental feeding, to increase stool output and bilirubin excretion [N2-F1].
- **Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIg)** may be considered if jaundice is related to blood type differences, although results are not conclusive [N2-F1].
- **Exchange transfusion** is reserved for severe jaundice that does not respond to other treatments [N2-F1].

### Infection and apnea workup and management
For infection, the workup should be prompt and includes blood culture, urine culture, and other cultures if needed, plus blood tests, lumbar puncture, and imaging if indicated [N4-F3]. The evidence states that newborn sepsis is diagnosed with blood culture as the main method, and treatment should start immediately with antibiotics even before test results are available [N4-F3]. The baby may need to stay in the NICU for close monitoring and supportive care, including fluids, oxygen, nutrition, and help with breathing [N4-F3].

For **apnea**, the evidence suggests that CPAP is used for apnea in preterm neonates when the infant continues to have apneic episodes [N5-R3]. CPAP is also described as a means of providing respiratory support for neonates with upper airway obstruction or respiratory failure [N5-R4]. The evidence also notes that CPAP has been shown to be relatively safe and effective in preventing and treating respiratory distress among preterm infants [N5-R1]. For apnea management, the workup would likely include respiratory assessment, oxygenation, and evaluation of underlying causes such as prematurity or airway obstruction.

- **Phototherapy** is used when jaundice is moderate or severe and bilirubin levels are high enough to require intervention [N2-F1]. Parents should watch for signs that may indicate a problem, including:
- **Jaundice**, especially if the yellow color spreads beyond the face [N2-F1]

- **Weight loss that is too much or too slow** [N3-F2]
- **Changes in behavior**, such as being very sleepy, fussy, or not eating well [N4-F3]
- **Fever or very low temperature** [N4-F3]
- **Abnormal breathing** or signs of respiratory distress [N4-F3]
- **Dehydration**, including fewer wet or poopy diapers than expected [N3-F2]
- **Lethargy, irritability, or poor feeding** [N1-R3][N4-R1]
- **Any unusual changes in the baby’s appearance, activity level, or alertness** [N2-F1]

Parents should call the doctor or return for care if the baby:
- Has **jaundice spreading beyond the face** [N2-F1]
- Is **not feeding well** [N3-F2]
- Has **poor feeding or refuses to eat** [N4-F3]
- Has **fever or very low temperature** [N4-F3]

- Has **unusual sleepiness, fussy behavior, or difficulty waking** [N4-F3]

## Differential diagnosis and urgency assessment for a 6-day-old full-term newborn

### Most likely conditions in a 6-day-old full-term newborn
In a 6-day-old full-term newborn, the most likely conditions are **jaundice**, **feeding difficulties**, and **infection/sepsis**, with **apnea** being less common but still relevant in certain clinical contexts. The evidence consistently identifies jaundice as extremely common in newborns, with about six out of 10 newborns having jaundice to varying degrees [N1-R2]. Neonatal jaundice is described as yellow coloring of the skin and eyes due to bilirubin buildup [N1-R1], and it is a leading reason for concern at this age [N1-R3]. Feeding problems are also common in newborns, especially in breastfed infants, and poor feeding can overlap with jaundice and infection [N1-R4][N3-R5]. Neonatal sepsis is another critical possibility, especially because newborns can develop signs rapidly and the infection may affect multiple body systems [N4-R1][N4-F3].

### Red flags that require immediate care
The red flags that require immediate care are the most serious signs of infection or severe disease. These include:
- **Fever or very low temperature** [N4-R2][N4-F3]
- **Poor feeding or refusing to eat** [N4-R2][N4-F3]
- **Unusual sleepiness or difficulty waking** [N4-R2][N4-F3]
- **Abnormal breathing or respiratory distress** [N4-R1][N4-F3]
- **Changes in behavior, such as being very sleepy, fussy, or not eating well** [N4-F3]
- **Changes in skin color or jaundice spreading beyond the face** [N2-F1]
- **Dehydration signs** [N3-F2]
- **Lethargy, irritability, or poor feeding** [N1-R3][N4-R1]

These signs are particularly urgent because they may indicate **neonatal sepsis**, **severe hyperbilirubinemia**, or other serious conditions requiring prompt evaluation [N4-F3][N1-R3]. The evidence also notes that jaundice should be assessed for clinical features of bilirubin encephalopathy, including poor feeding and lethargy, which are red flags for urgent jaundice management [N1-R3].

- **Jaundice** should be suspected when the baby’s skin and eyes appear yellow, especially after the first few days of life, when bilirubin levels peak [N1-R1][N2-F1]. - **Infection/sepsis** should be suspected when there is fever, low temperature, poor feeding, lethargy, or other signs of systemic illness [N4-R1][N4-F3]. The evidence also states that newborn sepsis can be hard to diagnose and may present with fever, changes in temperature, breathing problems, or digestive issues [N4-F3].

Feeding issues may overlap with jaundice because poor feeding can reduce stool output and delay bilirubin excretion, which worsens jaundice [N1-R4][N3-F2]. - **Few wet or poopy diapers** than expected for the baby’s age [N3-F2]
- **Lethargy, irritability, or poor alertness** during feedings [N3-F2]
- **Not waking for feedings** [N3-F2]

The evidence also states that frequent and effective breastfeeding helps the baby eliminate bilirubin and that poor feeding and not getting enough milk are risk factors for high bilirubin levels [N7-R2][N7-R5]. Breastfeeding support and feeding frequency are therefore central to recognizing and managing feeding concerns [N7-R2][N7-R5].

## Management and next steps
### Feeding support and hydration strategies
Feeding support should be individualized, with frequent feeding and hydration as the mainstays. For breastfed infants, the evidence strongly supports frequent breastfeeding, with 8 to 12 feedings a day for the first several days of life [N2-F1]. For formula-fed infants, the evidence recommends 1 to 2 ounces every 2 to 3 hours for the first week [N2-F1]. Poor feeding can also be managed with **supplemental feeding** if the baby is losing weight, dehydrated, or not feeding well [N2-F1]. The La Leche League Canada source emphasizes that scheduled feedings, swaddling, and pacifiers can reduce feeding cues, so feeding support should also focus on positioning, latching, and breastfeeding management [N3-F2]. If there is significant weight loss, positioning and latching need evaluation by an IBCLC, and supplementation may be required [N3-F2].

### Jaundice monitoring and treatment options
Jaundice should be monitored by assessing bilirubin levels and watching for progression of yellowing beyond the face [N2-F1]. The evidence states that jaundice often disappears on its own within two to three weeks, but moderate or severe jaundice may require prolonged hospital stay or readmission [N2-F1]. Treatment options include:
- **Phototherapy**, which is described as safe and effective for decreasing unconjugated bilirubin and reducing the need for exchange transfusion [N2-R3]. Mayo Clinic notes that phototherapy may be supplemented with light-emitting pads or mattresses [N2-R5].
- **Enhanced nutrition**, including more frequent feedings and supplemental feeding, to increase stool output and bilirubin excretion [N2-F1].
- **Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIg)** may be considered if jaundice is related to blood type differences, although results are not conclusive [N2-F1].
- **Exchange transfusion** is reserved for severe jaundice that does not respond to other treatments [N2-F1].

The evidence also notes that jaundice can be mild and self-limited, but bilirubin levels should guide treatment decisions [N2-F1].

### Infection and apnea workup and management
For infection, the workup should be prompt and includes blood culture, urine culture, and other cultures if needed, plus blood tests, lumbar puncture, and imaging if indicated [N4-F3]. The evidence states that newborn sepsis is diagnosed with blood culture as the main method, and treatment should start immediately with antibiotics even before test results are available [N4-F3]. The baby may need to stay in the NICU for close monitoring and supportive care, including fluids, oxygen, nutrition, and help with breathing [N4-F3].

For **apnea**, the evidence suggests that CPAP is used for apnea in preterm neonates when the infant continues to have apneic episodes [N5-R3]. CPAP is also described as a means of providing respiratory support for neonates with upper airway obstruction or respiratory failure [N5-R4]. The evidence also notes that CPAP has been shown to be relatively safe and effective in preventing and treating respiratory distress among preterm infants [N5-R1]. For apnea management, the workup would likely include respiratory assessment, oxygenation, and evaluation of underlying causes such as prematurity or airway obstruction.

### When to use phototherapy, CPAP, or supplemental feeding
- **Phototherapy** is used when jaundice is moderate or severe and bilirubin levels are high enough to require intervention [N2-F1]. The Mayo Clinic states that phototherapy should be instituted when the total serum bilirubin is at or above 15 mg/dL in infants 25 to 48 hours old [N2-R2]. The evidence also emphasizes that phototherapy is often the preferred treatment for neonatal hyperbilirubinemia [N2-R1].
- **CPAP** is used for apnea or respiratory support in neonates with upper airway obstruction or respiratory failure, especially when apnea persists [N5-R3][N5-R4]. It is also used in postextubation respiratory support [N5-R5].
- **Supplemental feeding** is used when the baby is not feeding well, is losing weight, is dehydrated, or when more nutrition is needed to support bilirubin excretion and growth [N2-F1][N3-F2]. The evidence recommends more-frequent feedings, supplementation, or formula feeding if breastfeeding is not sufficient [N2-F1].

## Bottom line for parents
In short, a 6-day-old full-term newborn is likely to be healthy, but parents should watch for jaundice, feeding problems, infection, or apnea. Jaundice is common but usually mild and self-limited; feeding problems can overlap with jaundice or infection; and infection or sepsis can develop rapidly with fever, poor feeding, or unusual behavior [N8][N9]. If any red flags appear, parents should call the doctor or return for care immediately [N8][N9]. Routine follow-up is important, and most babies do well with frequent feeding, consistent weight gain, and prompt attention to any changes [N10].
